facts.statement: Jiangxisaurus was an extinct oviraptorid theropod dinosaur found in the Late Cretaceous Nanxiong Formation of southern China.
facts.quote: Jiangxisaurus is an extinct genus of oviraptorid theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Nanxiong Formation of southern China.

facts.statement: Jiangxisaurus resembled Heyuannia but possessed more strongly curved front claws and a thinner, more fragile lower jaw.
facts.quote: It was similar to Heyuannia, but with more strongly curved anterior claws and a thinner, frailer mandible.

facts.statement: Jiangxisaurus was likely an omnivore, sharing this diet with its close relatives Nankangia and Ganzhousaurus.
facts.quote: It was most likely an omnivorous animal along with its close relatives Nankangia and Ganzhousaurus.

facts.statement: The genus Jiangxisaurus was described and named by Wei Xuefang, Pu Hanyong, Xu Li, Liu Di, and Lü Junchang in 2013.
facts.quote: Jiangxisaurus was described and named by Wei Xuefang, Pu Hanyong, Xu Li, Liu Di, and Lü Junchang in 2013

facts.statement: The genus name Jiangxisaurus honors Jiangxi Province, while the species name ganzhouensis refers to Ganzhou, the specific site of discovery.
facts.quote: The genus name Jiangxisaurus, refers to the Jiangxi Province of southern China. The specific name ganzhouensis, is derived from Ganzhou, the locality where the specimen was discovered.

facts.statement: The holotype skull of Jiangxisaurus measures 150mm in length and represents a sub-adult individual.
facts.quote: The skull is 150mm long and appears to be a sub-adult.

facts.statement: Jiangxisaurus had a toothless mandible with a height-to-length ratio of approximately 20%.
facts.quote: The mandible of Jiangxisaurus is toothless and has a height-to-length ratio of about 20%.

facts.statement: The radius of Jiangxisaurus is 96mm long, which is 30% shorter than its 136mm humerus.
facts.quote: The radius is 96mm in length and is 30% shorter than the length of the humerus (136mm).

facts.statement: The hand of Jiangxisaurus was tridactyl, featuring a robust first finger, an elongated second finger, and a slender third finger.
facts.quote: The manus is tridactyl, meaning that it has three fingers – the first digit is robust, the second is elongated and the third digit is slender.

facts.statement: Wei et al. (2013) identified Jiangxisaurus as a medium-sized oviraptorid with unique features including a weakly down-turned jaw symphysis, a concave suprangular bone, and a very elongated mandible.
facts.quote: According to Wei et al. (2013), Jiangxisaurus was a medium-sized oviraptorid dinosaur characterized by the following unique characters: the presence of a weakly down-turned mandibular symphysis a suprangular bone with an elongated and concave lateral surface a very elongated mandible, with a height-to-length ratio of about 20% a ratio of radius length to humerus length of about 70%

facts.statement: Jiangxisaurus is classified within the dinosaur family Oviraptoridae.
facts.quote: Jiangxisaurus was assigned to the taxon Oviraptoridae.

facts.statement: Jiangxisaurus lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 72 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: The specimen was collected in red sandstone sediments that were deposited during the Maastrichtian stage of the Cretaceous period, approximately 72 to 66 million years ago.

facts.statement: The only known specimen of Jiangxisaurus was found at the Nankang locality in Ganzhou City, Jiangxi Province, China.
facts.quote: The only known specimen of this genus was recovered at the Nankang locality of the Nanxiong Formation in Ganzhou City of Jiangxi Province, China.

facts.statement: Jiangxisaurus ganzhouensis is the only known species of this extinct genus, living in Asia during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 72 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Jiangxisaurus ganzhouensis es la única especie conocida del género extinto Jiangxisaurus de dinosaurio terópodo oviraptórido que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente entre 72 a 66 millones de años, durante el Maastrichtiense, en lo que es hoy Asia.

facts.statement: The discovery of Jiangxisaurus is paleontologically significant because it contributes to current knowledge about the paleogeographical distribution of oviraptorids in southern China.
facts.quote: Este hallazgo es paleontológicamente significativo porque contribuye al conocimiento actual sobre la distribución paleogeográfica de oviraptorides en el sur de China.

facts.statement: The specimen was collected from red sandstone sediments deposited during the Maastrichtian stage of the Cretaceous, approximately 72 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: El espécimen se recolectó en sedimentos de arenisca roja que se depositaron durante la etapa Maastrichtiense del Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 72 a 66 millones de años.

facts.statement: The Nanxiong Formation consists of a 2000-meter sequence of red sandstones and clays that has yielded dinosaur fossils, footprints, and abundant eggshells.
facts.quote: La Formación Nanxiong consiste en una secuencia de areniscas y arcillas de 2000 metros que ha dado lugar a fósiles de dinosaurios, huellas de dinosaurios y abundantes cáscaras de huevo.

facts.statement: Jiangxisaurus was assigned to the taxon Oviraptoridae and shares traits with other oviraptorids such as a short, narrow skull with a toothless jaw.
facts.quote: Jiangxisaurus fue asignado al taxón Oviraptoridae. Este género comparte varios rasgos con otros oviraptóridos, incluido un cráneo estrecho y corto con una mandíbula sin dientes y vértebras cervicales anteriores con pleurocoelos.

facts.statement: The time range for Jiangxisaurus is the Maastrichtian, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Maastrichtian (72.2 to 66 million years ago)
